description: Offline research snapshot for a simulated Health NZ National Office recruitment assistant. The March 2025 OIA appendix contributes full-text, scope-labelled chunks of a July 2022 National Office recruitment policy and a people-leader guide; older Counties Manukau pages are excluded. Released National Office Code of Conduct and Privacy Policy clauses are also included. Current policy status is unverified. Public guidance summaries are labelled separately. Health NZ source text was extracted and reformatted for retrieval.

policy.title: Health NZ application, recruitment and pre-employment checks
policy.source_note: Research summary of Health NZ's public careers page; not an internal recruitment policy.
policy.text: Applicants use Health NZ's official careers sites to review vacancy details and submit a CV and cover letter. Recruitment teams provide updates and next steps. Pre-employment checks vary by role and can include references, work history, identity, right to work, professional registration, police vetting or health screening. Do not imply every check applies to every role. Health NZ does not ask candidates to pay for a job or fast-track an offer.

policy.title: Health NZ privacy notice for job applicants
policy.source_note: Research summary of Health NZ's published applicant privacy notice.
policy.text: Health NZ collects application information such as CVs, cover letters and records of recruitment contact. Some information is necessary to assess an application; other information is optional. Recruitment information should be used and shared for the recruitment purposes described in the notice. Check the full notice when answering a detailed privacy request.

policy.text: 10. Recruiting staff from a range of diverse backgrounds, experiences, skills and perspectives adds considerable value to Te Whatu Ora and the services it offers. policy.text: 33. policy.title: Health NZ people-leader recruitment guide: Before recruiting
policy.text: Before you recruit: Do you want to recruit new talent for your team? The first step to start your recruitment journey is to reach out to your friendly HR Business Partner (HRBP). They’re here to help you assess your recruitment needs including the position type and salary band for your vacant position. Your HRBP will help you through the steps below, so you’ll be ready to embark on the exciting journey of finding the perfect candidate for your team. Step 1 - Position Description: First, let's determine if this is a new position or an existing one. If it's a new position or you don't have a current Position Description (PD), don't worry! You can use our easy-to-use Position Description template to prepare one. Once you have drafted your PD, you can send it to your HRBP for review. They will make sure it aligns with your team's needs and won't have any impact on existing positions. Some new positions will need to be sized so the salary range offered is appropriate. Your HRBP can talk you through the requirements and the process. The job sizing committee meets every week, so make sure to submit your Position Description to your HRBP by the end of business, on a Thursday. Missing this deadline means your position will be sized the following week.

policy.title: Health NZ people-leader recruitment guide: Interview preparation
policy.text: Interviews: Interviews are a key part of the recruitment process. This is the first real chance your candidate has to meet their prospective new organisation, manager and colleagues. To ensure fairness and eliminate biases, it's recommended to have a panel of two to three interviewers. This minimises biased hiring and allows for impartial assessments. It also enables the interview panel to compare their notes afterwards, ensuring accuracy and fair rating scores. Your interview panel must consist of: • People Leader (you) • Any team members who understand your service and the position Interview Questions Your Recruitment Consultant can provide you with a tailored interview guide with questions based on the competency requirements of the position. Interview Notes Your interview notes contain valuable insights about your candidate’s strengths, skills, and areas where they have potential for growth. Once you have completed the interviews, please send your interview notes to your Recruitment Consultant for safekeeping. Setting the interview scene We want to ensure that the interview process is a great experience for your candidate. Remember the candidate is interviewing us as well and trying to establish if you and your team are a good fit for them.

policy.title: Health NZ people-leader recruitment guide: Interview preparation
policy.text: Before the interview: The panel will receive a copy of the interview questions, Position Description, candidate's CV, Cover Letter, and any other application documents from the Recruitment team once your interviews have been confirmed. Ensure your panel members arrive at least ten minutes early so you can discuss who will ask which questions and how the interview will be managed. If your interviews are in person: • Set up the interview room so there is enough space for the candidate and the interview panel. • Make sure the tables are clean, and there are enough chairs for everyone. • Offer a glass of water to your candidate on arrival. • Your panel and candidate should sit around the table - it’s not an interrogation, it’s a conversation.

policy.title: Health NZ people-leader recruitment guide: Interview conduct and accommodation
policy.text: During the interview: • The People Leader should welcome the candidate, guide them to their seat (if in person), and introduce themself and the panel members. • Explain to the candidate how the interview is going to be conducted and how long the interview should take. • Remind the candidate that you will be taking notes, so apologise if you are not making eye contact during the interview. All interview notes must be professional, appropriate, and legible (these are all discoverable). • Take a few minutes to introduce our company and run through the details of the role. This is your opportunity to shine a light on the positive attributes of this position and the culture within the team. • After asking the opening questions, the People Leader should inform the candidate that they will now proceed with the formal interview questions. • The People Leader should lead the interview. Allow the conversation to flow naturally and avoid reading the questions verbatim. Feel free to ask follow-up questions and dig deeper into areas of interest. • Keep an eye on the time to ensure you’re able to get through all the questions. • Ask for the candidate's referees and let them know that you will be in touch with them before contacting reference checks.

policy.text: Rescheduling an interview If you need to reschedule an interview, please be considerate of your candidate's situation and provide reasonable notice. In the event of an unforeseen circumstance requiring a last-minute rescheduling, the People Leader should contact the candidate directly to inform them about the cancellation and arrange a new interview time. Let your Recruitment Consultant know the new interview date and time so they can update any Teams invitations or special accommodations. Candidate Talent Pool When it comes to interviewing candidates for a vacancy, you might come across candidates who really stand out and impress you. If you find yourself thinking, "This person would be a great fit for another team" or "I would definitely hire them if I had another vacancy," ask them if they would like to be added to our Talent Pool and let your Recruitment Consultant know. The Talent Pool system allows us to add these promising candidates to our database and keep them informed about any suitable future vacancies that arise. By sharing your insights, we can ensure that these talented individuals don't miss out on exciting opportunities within our organisation.

policy.title: Health NZ people-leader recruitment guide: Talent pool and reference checks
policy.text: Reference Checks: Now that your interviews are all wrapped up, it's time to embark on the next step: completing reference checks for your preferred candidate. Reference checks play a crucial role in validating the information gathered during the interviews and provide an opportunity to hear from previous managers about their experience with the candidate. As the People Leader, you will be responsible for conducting reference checks. Don't worry, we've got two convenient options for you: conducting them online through Checkmate or verbal reference checks using our Reference Check form. If you prefer the online option, simply let your Recruitment Consultant know, and they will guide you through the process. During the interview, remember to ask for permission to contact the candidate's referees. Once you've made your decision on the preferred candidate, give them a call to confirm you can reach out to those referees. For privacy reasons, you may only contact referees provided by the candidate. This includes internal candidates. Please note reference checks should only be conducted on the preferred candidate, not for all candidates.

If they do not wish to provide their current manager as a referee, a previous manager may be satisfactory. Please discuss with your Recruitment Consultant if you are unsure. • Internal candidate: It is recommended to conduct at least one reference check, preferably with their current manager. If you have any questions about reference checks, don’t hesitate to contact your Recruitment Consultant. Making an offer: Now that you have completed the reference checks for your candidate, it's time to pick up the phone and talk to your candidate about an upcoming offer! During this conversation, you'll have the opportunity to discuss and negotiate employment terms, salary, start date, and more. Once your candidate has agreed that they are satisfied with the terms you discuss, contact your Recruitment Consultant, and they will send you a Staff Appointment Form (SAF) to complete. This form will then be sent to your manager for approval.

Double-check the important details like the candidate's name, the role being offered, salary, start date, and any additional benefits. • Timing and method: Choose a time that works for both you and the candidate to discuss the details of the potential offer. policy.title: Health NZ National Office Privacy Policy (clause 7)
policy.text: 7. The following definitions are used for the purposes of this policy: Health Information “Health information” is a subset of personal information, where the information is about an identifiable individual’s health. This includes information about their health or disabilities, their medical history, health or disability services provided to them, and information collected while providing health and disability services, such as addresses for billing purposes or information relevant to funding. Examples of health information are: clinical notes, genetic information, test results, diagnostic images, verbal discussion and records of conversations. This includes information about living individuals and can include information about deceased individuals. Personal Information “Personal information” means information about a living identifiable individual. This information can be in any form, including paper and electronic documents and files, emails, personnel records and patient records, and can include images such as photos, an image of a pathology report or a diagnostic image. It can also include video recordings and audio recordings.

policy.title: Health NZ National Office Privacy Policy (clause 7)
policy.text: Examples of personal information include an individual’s name, telephone number, address (email and postal), date of birth, ethnic origin, tax number and Health Information. Even if an individual’s name does not appear in information, but there is a reasonable chance that an individual could be identified from the information (including where information can be combined with other information to identify a person), it can still be personal information for the purposes of the Privacy Act. Privacy Breach A “privacy breach” occurs when personal information held by Te Whatu Ora is accessed, disclosed, altered, lost or destroyed without authorisation or by accident, or when requests for access or correction to personal information are not processed in a timely manner. This includes internal misuse of information, such as browsing of personal information or inappropriate sharing of personal information with colleagues who have no work-related purpose to access it. A privacy breach may also be something that prevents Te Whatu Ora from accessing the information on a temporary or permanent basis. Privacy Incident A “privacy incident” is any incident that may be, or that could have led to, a privacy breach. This includes near misses.

policy.title: Health NZ National Office Privacy Policy (clause 39)
policy.text: 39. An individual is entitled to complain to the Office of the Privacy Commissioner if they consider that an action of Te Whatu Ora is an interference with their privacy. For an action to be an interference with privacy, there must have been a breach of one or more of the IPPS (or of an information sharing or matching agreement), or a failure to give notice of a privacy breach. The action must also have caused loss, detriment, damage, on injury to the individual, adversely affected (or may adversely affect) their rights, benefits, obligations, or interests, or resulted in (or may result in) significant humiliation, significant loss of dignity, or significant injury to the individual's feelings. The Privacy Commissioner may investigate such complaints, may try to settle the complaint, and may refer complaints to the Director of Proceedings.

policy.title: Public Service Commission merit-based employment decisions
policy.source_note: Research summary of 29 June 2026 guidance, which supports Crown entities under the Crown Entities Act; it creates no new obligations.
policy.text: Define merit from the skills, experience and thinking needed for the role. Use fair, evidence-based processes that comply with privacy and other legal requirements. Describe role requirements accurately and review appointment recommendations before finalising them. The guidance recognises that reasonable decision makers may differ, so keep assessment evidence and the rationale open to review.

policy.title: Public Service Commission workforce assurance model standards
policy.source_note: Research summary of the Commission's workforce assurance standards for public service departments and statutory Crown entities; use the official source for full requirements.
policy.text: Recruitment screening should include checks proportionate to the role and clear responsibilities for anyone performing them, including a third-party provider. Tell applicants that screening will occur and why, and obtain the relevant consent to seek information. Referee and integrity checks are normally completed at the preferred-candidate stage before contractual relations form. Where serious misconduct information is relevant, follow the standards and agreed information-sharing process rather than informally contacting people outside the process.

policy.title: Employment New Zealand discrimination guidance
policy.source_note: Research summary of Employment New Zealand guidance; use the source for the current law and exceptions.
policy.text: Employment discrimination may be direct or indirect. Recruitment decisions should be based on job requirements rather than assumptions about protected characteristics. A neutral-looking rule may disadvantage a protected group, so consider whether it is genuinely required for the work. Assess the actual experience and capability shown by each applicant.

policy.title: Immigration New Zealand right-to-work checks
policy.source_note: Research summary of employer guidance; visa conditions vary and must be checked for the particular person and job.
policy.text: Before a person from overseas starts work, the employer must check that their visa allows the proposed work. VisaView is one way for registered employers to verify entitlement. A temporary visa may permit work, but restrictions can depend on employer, role, location and duration. Do not equate citizenship or residence with the only lawful ways to work. If entitlement is unclear, refer it for verification rather than assume.

policy.title: Office of the Privacy Commissioner privacy principles
policy.source_note: Research summary of the Privacy Act 2020 principles; check the source for qualifications and exceptions.
policy.text: Collect necessary personal information fairly and tell people why it is collected. Protect it, use it for the collected purpose, limit disclosure and retention, and take care with accuracy. People may request access to and correction of their information. Principle 12 concerns disclosure outside New Zealand; Principle 13 concerns unique identifiers. Applicant records and screening notes can contain personal information.
